title: Eczema (Vicharchika): Ayurvedic View, Triggers, Diet & Skin Care
excerpt: Dry skin, red patches, intense itching, sometimes oozing and then crusting — eczema troubles both children and adults. Learn what eczema is, how Ayurveda understands it as “Vicharchika”, what sets it off, what to eat and avoid, daily skin care, safe home measures and when you must see a doctor immediately.
content:
“The itching is so bad at night that I can’t sleep, and scratching peels the skin” — many parents tell us this about their children, and adults about themselves. According to the UK’s National Health Service (NHS), atopic eczema affects around 1 in 5 children and 1 in 10 adults there; it is common in India too.

Eczema is not contagious. With the right care, avoiding triggers and treatment, it can be kept largely under control. This article is for information only — take any treatment only on the advice of your vaidya or doctor.

What is Eczema?

Eczema (dermatitis) is a long-lasting inflammatory skin condition in which the skin’s protective barrier weakens, moisture escapes quickly and the skin gets irritated easily. Its main types are:

  • Atopic eczema — the most common; often starts in childhood, with a family history of allergy, asthma or sneezing
  • Contact dermatitis — from contact with something, such as soap, detergent, cement, imitation jewellery, hair dye or rubber
  • Hand and foot eczema — from frequent work with water, soap or chemicals; sometimes tiny fluid-filled bumps

It keeps flaring and settling. In children it often appears on the cheeks, the folds of elbows and knees and the neck; in adults on the hands, feet and skin folds. Ringworm (fungal infection), psoriasis and scabies can look similar, so do not put cream on every itchy rash yourself — get the correct diagnosis first.

The Ayurvedic View

In Ayurveda, skin diseases are grouped under Kushtha, and one of the Kshudra Kushtha (minor skin diseases) is Vicharchika, which closely matches today’s eczema. Acharya Charaka describes it in a single line:

सकण्डूपिडका श्यावा बहुस्रावा विचर्चिका ।
— Charaka Samhita, Chikitsa Sthana 7

Meaning: A condition with itching and eruptions (bumps), where the skin turns dusky-dark (shyava) and there is a lot of discharge (oozing), is called “Vicharchika”.

According to Ayurveda, in Vicharchika the main dosha is Kapha, along with Pitta and vitiated rakta (blood). The causes described include viruddha ahara (incompatible food, such as milk with fish, salt or sour fruits), very heavy and oily food, suppressing natural urges, daytime sleep and mental stress. So the aim of treatment is to improve agni, purify the blood, keep the skin unctuous (moist) from inside and outside, and avoid the triggering causes.

Main Causes and Triggers

  • Family history of eczema, allergy, asthma or sneezing
  • Dry skin — bathing in very hot water, frequent soap, dry winter air
  • Harsh soaps, detergents, perfumed lotions, hair dye, cement, imitation jewellery
  • Woollen or synthetic clothes, excessive sweating, dust, house dust mites and pet hair
  • Stress, lack of sleep and skin infections
  • Certain foods in some people — but this differs from person to person and is known only through testing

Symptoms and Tests

  • Intense itching that gets worse at night
  • Dry, rough, red or darkening skin
  • Small bumps or blisters that ooze fluid and then crust
  • Skin becoming thick and lined from long-term scratching
  • Cracks, burning and pain in the skin of the hands
  • In children, irritability and broken sleep due to itching

In most cases the doctor or vaidya recognises it just by looking at the skin. If needed, a fungal test (skin scraping), a test for infection, a patch test for contact allergy or blood tests may be advised. If a food allergy is suspected in children, do testing and avoidance only under a doctor’s supervision — stopping many foods on your own can harm a child’s nutrition.

Diet: What to Eat, What to Avoid

In eczema, the aim of diet is to keep agni healthy, avoid incompatible food and nourish the skin. According to Ayurveda, light, fresh, easily digestible food and bitter-tasting vegetables are considered beneficial in skin diseases.

What to eat

  • Old rice, wheat, barley, moong dal — light, freshly cooked food
  • Vegetables such as bitter gourd, pointed gourd, bottle gourd, ridge gourd, tinda; turmeric in food
  • Seasonal fruits such as papaya, pomegranate, apple (those that suit you)
  • A little desi ghee in food — for inner unctuousness of the skin (ask your doctor if you have heart disease or high cholesterol)
  • Enough water through the day
  • A light dinner at the right time

What to avoid

  • Incompatible food — milk with fish, salty snacks or sour fruits; milk and curd together
  • Very sour, spicy, fried food, pickles, stale and packaged food
  • Too many sweets, refined flour, junk food, alcohol and smoking
  • Any food you see repeatedly flaring your eczema — identify it and avoid it on the advice of your doctor/vaidya

Daily Skin Care and Routine

  • Bathe in lukewarm (not hot) water for 5–10 minutes; use a mild, fragrance-free cleanser instead of soap
  • Pat the skin dry after bathing and apply moisturiser or plain oil within 3 minutes; repeat 2–3 times a day
  • Wear loose cotton clothes; do not wear woollens directly on the skin
  • Keep nails short; when it itches, apply a cool compress or press gently instead of scratching — children can wear cotton gloves at night
  • Wear gloves while washing dishes and clothes; use a mild detergent and rinse clothes well
  • Reduce stress, sleep on time; do not keep the room very hot or dry

Yoga and Pranayama

Anulom-Vilom, Bhramari, Sheetali pranayama and meditation are considered helpful in reducing stress and the itch cycle; among poses, Bhujangasana, Marjari Asana, Balasana and Shavasana. Caution: heavy sweating can flare eczema, so do gentle yoga and afterwards bathe in lukewarm water and apply moisturiser; avoid poses that strain cracked or oozing skin; learn yoga from a trained teacher.

Safe Home Measures

  • Plain oil or moisturiser: pure coconut or sesame oil, or a fragrance-free moisturiser — test on a small area first
  • Cool compress: during itching, soak a clean cloth in cool water and hold it on for a few minutes
  • Turmeric in food: turmeric in food is fine, but do not apply raw turmeric or any paste directly on the skin — it can cause irritation
  • Sleep and stress: meditation or pranayama before bed, to break the itch-scratch cycle

Do not apply lemon, camphor, kerosene, toothpaste or any home paste on cracked skin. Market “ringworm-itch” mixed creams often contain strong steroids that, over time, thin the skin and make the disease stubborn — avoid them without a doctor’s advice.

Ayurvedic Treatment — With Caution

Ayurveda mentions many medicines for Kushtha and Vicharchika, such as Neem, Manjishtha, Khadira, Haridra (turmeric), Guduchi, Triphala, and classical formulations like Mahamanjishthadi Kwath. After examination, when suitable, Shodhana (such as Virechana), and the clinic’s Jaloka Therapy (leech therapy) and Raktamokshana may be advised. However:

  • Which medicine or procedure, in what amount and for how long — this is decided by the vaidya only after looking at the stage of disease, age, constitution, pulse and current medicines.
  • Do not stop medicines or creams prescribed by your doctor on your own — especially stopping steroid creams or tablets suddenly can cause a sharp flare; reduce them gradually and only on your doctor’s advice.
  • Some herbs and oils can cause skin allergy or change the effect of other medicines, so tell your vaidya the list of all your medicines; avoid unlabelled “miracle skin medicines”.
  • During pregnancy and breastfeeding, and for infants, children and the elderly, take any medicine or procedure only on the advice of a vaidya/doctor. Beware of claims like “eczema cured from the root”.

When to See a Doctor Immediately

  • Sudden painful clusters of blisters on eczema, with fever or lethargy — go to a hospital immediately (this can be a serious viral infection)
  • Yellow crusts, pus, spreading redness, swelling or pain — signs of bacterial skin infection
  • Eczema around the eyes with eye pain, redness or blurred vision
  • An infant with eczema who is not feeding, not gaining weight or very irritable
  • Redness spreading rapidly over the whole body, chills or peeling skin
  • Persistent sleeplessness due to itching, or no improvement in 2–3 weeks despite treatment

Summary — Points to Remember

  • Eczema is not contagious — it can be kept under control with the right care
  • Daily moisture — a lukewarm bath followed immediately by moisturiser or plain oil
  • Identify your triggers: harsh soap, detergent, woollens, sweat, stress
  • Less incompatible, very sour, spicy and fried food; light, fresh meals
  • Avoid market mixed steroid creams; medicines and procedures like Jaloka only under a qualified vaidya
